title: New Book Chronicle (review of Odler, Copper in Ancient Egypt: before, during and after the Pyramid Age, c. 4000-1600 BC)
ask_addressed: What is documented about pharaonic Egyptian copper, gold and bronze metallurgy, dyes and pigments (Egyptian green/frit), and the medical papyri (Ebers, Edwin Smith) that bear on chemistry?
quote: bronze (an alloy of copper and tin) was actually very rare
summary: Review of a 2023 monograph on Egyptian copper: bronze was rare in the 'Bronze Age', arsenical copper far more widespread, ores processed near Eastern Desert and Sinai mines.
limits: A review of a book, not the book; reviewer not identified in the text opened; covers c. 4000-1600 BC only, so not the New Kingdom.

title: New Book Chronicle (review of Odler, Copper in Ancient Egypt)
ask_addressed: What is documented about pharaonic Egyptian copper, gold and bronze metallurgy, dyes and pigments (Egyptian green/frit), and the medical papyri (Ebers, Edwin Smith) that bear on chemistry?
quote: for a century the hieroglyph for "copper" was misinterpreted by scholars as meaning "crucible"
summary: Shows how Egyptological reading of the vocabulary of copper and metalworkers was corrected; relevant to claims of a pharaonic 'chemical' vocabulary.
limits: Second-hand report of the monograph's philological chapter; no primary texts examined here.

title: The History of Ancient Technology (Presidential Address)
venue: Bulletin of the British Society for the History of Science 1(4)
ask_addressed: What is documented about pharaonic Egyptian copper, gold and bronze metallurgy, dyes and pigments (Egyptian green/frit), and the medical papyri (Ebers, Edwin Smith) that bear on chemistry?
quote: this name, asem, is perhaps the oldest name of a metal to be recorded
summary: Surveys ancient applied chemistry; notes the Egyptian name asem for electrum, attested from the First Dynasty on his account, and unrefined early gold.
limits: 1950 address, a 'rapid and rather superficial survey' by his own words; dates and claims predate modern analyses and must be checked against current work.

title: The History of Ancient Technology (Presidential Address)
venue: Bulletin of the British Society for the History of Science 1(4)
ask_addressed: Is there any Egyptological statement on whether pharaonic Egypt had alchemy or a written chemistry before the Greek-Roman period? Include sceptical views.
quote: some kind of refining process was used in Asia Minor about 1400 B.C., long before its use in Lydia in 550 B.C.
summary: Argues from Amarna-letter evidence that gold refining was known in the Near East by about 1400 BC but infers Egyptian methods of refining and testing gold were not well known then; frames ancient chemistry as applied craft.
limits: Old, inferential, and the Amarna letters concern Near Eastern correspondence, not Egyptian written chemistry; does not discuss alchemy proper.

title: Egyptian blue: modern myths, ancient realities
authors: Skovmoller, A., Brons, C., Sargent, M. L.
ask_addressed: What is documented about pharaonic Egyptian copper, gold and bronze metallurgy, dyes and pigments (Egyptian green/frit), and the medical papyri (Ebers, Edwin Smith) that bear on chemistry?
quote: Egyptian blue is a calcium copper tetrasilicate compound, a synthetic pigment made by heating a calcium compound
summary: Only the Cambridge abstract/extract was opened: composition and recipe of the synthetic blue frit and cobalt 'Amarna-blue'.
limits: Abstract only (paywall). Concerns Egyptian blue, not green frit; Mediterranean and Roman focus.

title: Simply red: A Late Bronze Age glass ingot from Amarna
authors: Jackson, C. M., Nicholson, P. T.
ask_addressed: What is documented about pharaonic Egyptian copper, gold and bronze metallurgy, dyes and pigments (Egyptian green/frit), and the medical papyri (Ebers, Edwin Smith) that bear on chemistry?
quote: shows an excess of copper colourant which indicates that the intended colour was opaque red
summary: Chemical analysis of an ingot from Amarna: evidence for deliberate colouring with copper in New Kingdom glassmaking, linked to Qantir refractory remains and Amarna furnaces.
limits: Glass, not frit or pigment; one object; CC BY open copy. Printed DOI not read from the page copy, so omitted.

title: Magic and Medicine

quote: The Ebers papyrus prescribes invocations to be uttered when taking a dose of medicine
summary: Presents the Ebers pharmacopoeia as mixing invocations with nauseous remedies; names Smith papyrus as mainly surgical.
limits: 1953 essay with dated language ('primitive man'); extract only; not a chemical analysis of ingredients.

title: Commentary on the Significance for Modern Neurology of the 17th Century B.C. Surgical Papyrus
venue: Canadian Journal of Neurological Sciences 14, pp. 560-563
ask_addressed: What is documented about pharaonic Egyptian copper, gold and bronze metallurgy, dyes and pigments (Egyptian green/frit), and the medical papyri (Ebers, Edwin Smith) that bear on chemistry?
quote: it contains the earliest mention in oriental literature of (a) the brain and meninges
summary: Summarises Breasted's 1930 edition of the Edwin Smith papyrus and its dating; bears on empirical medicine, not chemistry.
limits: About neurology and surgery; says nothing about chemical practice. Its interpretation follows Breasted and may overstate 'rational' medicine.

title: Ancient handbooks and Graeco-Egyptian collections of alchemical recipes
ask_addressed: Is there any Egyptological statement on whether pharaonic Egypt had alchemy or a written chemistry before the Greek-Roman period? Include sceptical views.
quote: two anonymous recipe books on papyrus codices written in third- or fourth-century Egypt
summary: Treats the Leiden and Stockholm papyri as the earliest alchemical recipe compilations, dated to the third or fourth century CE, not the pharaonic period.
limits: Does not itself assert a pharaonic absence; the date of the written corpus is the point. Recipe content may draw on older craft practice.

title: Alchemy and Translation (Chapter 12, Companion to Medieval Translation)
ask_addressed: Is there any Egyptological statement on whether pharaonic Egypt had alchemy or a written chemistry before the Greek-Roman period? Include sceptical views.
quote: The Leiden and Stockholm papyri, composed in third-century Egypt, contain 255 Greek recipes
summary: Describes the earliest extant alchemical writing as Greek recipes for dyes, imitation stones and gilded or silvered metals from Roman Egypt.
limits: Overview chapter, abstract/first page only; focus is later translation.

title: A Survey of Greek Alchemy
ask_addressed: Is there any Egyptological statement on whether pharaonic Egypt had alchemy or a written chemistry before the Greek-Roman period? Include sceptical views.
quote: Arising perhaps in the traditional knowledge of the Egyptian priesthood
summary: Proposes, with hedging, a priestly Egyptian origin while noting the earliest surviving alchemical works are all in Greek.
limits: 1930 extract; 'perhaps' is speculation, not evidence of pharaonic alchemy, and no pharaonic text is cited in the extract.

title: The Visions of Zosimos of Panopolis: Text, Translation, and Commentary
ask_addressed: Is there any Egyptological statement on whether pharaonic Egypt had alchemy or a written chemistry before the Greek-Roman period? Include sceptical views.
quote: being preserved and transmitted through temple traditions and their priests, from Old Kingdom Egypt to the Late Antique period
summary: Reports Zosimos's own view of a primordial alchemical tradition running from the Old Kingdom through temples; thesis relays that as Zosimos's belief.
limits: The Old Kingdom claim is Zosimos's third-century CE assertion, not independent evidence of pharaonic alchemy. Doctoral thesis, not peer reviewed.
